headline: PHAC Executive Committee heard a presentation on New Hampshire Care Connections and closed-loop referrals, with no votes taken.
summary: Unite Us presented an overview of New Hampshire Care Connections, a state-sponsored referral network, covering funding, governance, regional implementation, and contract terms through September 2029. The Healthy Aging/Aging Adult Committee gave updates on a resource guide, a Quality of Life Survey launching October 1, and a Resource Center planned for October. The next meeting is scheduled for December 21, 2026.

Minutes 
Introductions   Members introduced themselves and described their roles in their respective 
organizations.  
Presentation by 
Unite US 
New Hampshire Care Connections Overview 
 It was explained that the presentation would cover New Hampshire Care 
Connections and closed-loop referrals, while emphasizing the importance of 
learning about PHAC members’ prior experiences with similar initiatives. She 
introduced the state-sponsored initiative as a network of healthcare and 
service providers working to improve care coordination, with Unite Us serving 
as the platform for closed-loop referrals. 
Care Connections Components and Unite Us Functions 
 The presenters described the initiative’s funding and collaborators, including 
New Hampshire DHHS, the Department of Military Affairs and Veteran 
Services, Unite Us, Granite United Way, and 211 New Hampshire. They 
explained that Granite United Way supports the resource directory, 
assistance request forms linked to a community health worker, and 
communications, education, outreach, and strategy. The presentation then 
reviewed Unite Us capabilities, including referrals, screening and intake 
forms, and data access for monitoring outcomes. 
History and Evolution of Closed-Loop Referral 
 Reviewed the history of closed-loop referral efforts in New Hampshire, 
including the 2021 Unite Us pilot, its COVID-era funding, and its focus on 
behavioral and mental health providers. The discussion emphasized lessons 
learned from attempting statewide implementation and the shift toward 
regionally based networks built on existing partnerships. 
Governance, Access, and Contract Structure 
 The group discussed the stronger governance model supporting the current 
initiative, including DHHS coordination, an advisory council, and data review. 
Participants clarified account reactivation requirements, updated consent 
rules, the contract term through September 2029, and the performance-

based basis for a possible five-year extension. 
Regional Anchors and Champions 
 Discussion on the regional implementation model and the Upper Valley’s 
progress from pilot build-out toward ramp-up. The discussion defined 
anchors as organizations that generate significant referral activity and 
champions as organizations that support outreach, education, coordination, 
and regional engagement. 
Public Health Network Discovery and Cohort Planning 
 Granite United Way’s engagement with New Hampshire’s 13 regional public 
health networks was described as a discovery process to understand local 
history, needs, and readiness. A quarterly RPHN cohort scheduled to launch 
in October will provide updates, share data and success stories, support peer 
learning, and communicate regional feedback to DHHS. 
Comments/ 
Questions 
 Regional Planning and Request for Concrete Examples-The project team 
explained that regions with sufficient interest and capacity may receive 
support to identify anchors, champions, priority populations, and initial 
community-readiness steps.  
 Discussion on how hospitals and health systems can participate when they 
already use an EHR. It was explained that health systems can serve as anchors 
and may receive technical support for integration. Dartmouth’s phased 
expansion and potential Nashua participation were also discussed. 
 The meeting reviewed active referral and handoff patterns across New 
Hampshire, highlighting Dartmouth’s Upper Valley network, its regional 
recruitment strategy, and the growth of participating organizations. Speakers 
also described phased onboarding of aging and disability resource centers and 
strong participation by AmeriHealth and Well Sense. 
 Participants explored whether closed-loop referrals could support 
coordinated entry and food-security work. Coordinated entry was viewed as a 
longer-term opportunity because of its administrative complexity, while food-
access organizations could use resource shares and local navigators when 
they lack the capacity to manage facilitated referrals. 
 Discussion on prior implementation challenges, including referrals that simply 
directed clients to call for screening and limited feedback on outcomes.  
 It was emphasized that implementation models must reflect differences 
between large systems and small nonprofits, particularly in staffing, funding, 
workflow, and technical capacity. It was urged to help essential organizations 
overcome barriers to participation.
3 | P a g e  
 
Healthy Aging / 
Aging Adult 
Committee Update 
 Healthy Aging: Committee is developing an older adult resource guide and 
expanding access to incontinence products. 
 Quality of Life Survey: Survey is being translated into Spanish and Portuguese, 
with a target launch of October 1. Results will help identify needs and service 
gaps. 
 Home Safety: A home safety/fall prevention assessment was shared for 
possible use with older adults. 
 Scam Prevention: Members discussed increasing scams targeting older adults 
and an upcoming scam prevention workshop. 
 Resource Center: Public Health and Harbor Care are planning to launch a 
Resource Center in October to connect residents with community services. 
 Next Steps: Continue survey distribution, analyze results, and involve partners 
in the Resource Center, feasibility study, and gap analysis. 
 
 
Next Meeting December 21, 2026
